EMNLP 2023Learning from new knowledge

ALCUNA: Large Language Models Meet New Knowledge

Xunjian Yin*, Baizhou Huang*, Xiaojun Wan

Paper ↗arXiv ↗Code ↗

ALCUNA creates fictional organisms to test knowledge that models have not memorized, exposing a gap between reading new facts and connecting them to existing knowledge.

01 / The research question

Novelty has to be controlled

A benchmark about new knowledge faces a basic identification problem: a model may answer because it memorized the entity, because it understood the supplied description, or because a familiar name suggested a plausible guess. ALCUNA makes novelty part of the experimental design. It creates artificial biological entities whose properties can be traced back to a controlled transformation of an existing knowledge graph.

The construction preserves enough biological structure for the questions to remain meaningful. Properties shared by a class are retained, while selected attributes and relationships change. This produces a harder test than inventing an arbitrary name with an unrelated list of facts: the new entity resembles something the model already knows, so familiar knowledge can help with reasoning but can also interfere with the new description.

02 / Inside the method

A missing fact is also a test

KnowGen uses four operations: inherit a property, vary its value, extend the entity with a related property, or drop a property. The paper's example starts from Alpaca: the new entity keeps a leaf diet, changes body mass from 60 to 56.5 kilograms, drops lifespan, and gains a first-appearance property from a related species. Each operation gives the evaluator a specific expectation about the answer.

Dropping lifespan is especially revealing. The description does not authorize copying the parent's lifespan, even if that value is readily available from memory. A correct response must distinguish an unspecified fact from an inherited one. Association questions add another requirement: follow a relationship from the artificial entity into existing knowledge, then complete the reasoning chain using a fact that was not repeated in the new description.

To isolate this last ability, the authors check whether each model already answers the prerequisite questions about existing entities. Association evaluation is filtered accordingly. Question templates are also generated before the artificial entity is inserted. These controls help separate failures to combine available facts from failures caused by an unknown prerequisite or a template that accidentally reveals the answer.

  1. 01

    Create unfamiliar entities

    KnowGen modifies attributes and relations in biological taxonomy data to generate artificial organisms with controlled connections to real entities.

  2. 02

    Separate three abilities

    Evaluate understanding, differentiation, and association with questions that require progressively more interaction between supplied facts and existing knowledge.

  3. 03

    Vary the context

    Compare prompting settings, entity similarity, and additional context to identify where models confuse or fail to connect knowledge.

03 / Reading the evidence

The bottleneck is integration

  • 75.44%

    Understanding

    ChatGPT's knowledge-understanding score with vanilla few-shot prompting; reading the supplied facts is the stronger capability in this comparison.

  • 41.52%

    Association

    The same model and prompting setup score much lower when answers require connecting the new entity to existing knowledge.

The ablations make the benchmark more informative than a single average score. For ChatGLM, the association score rises from 27.47 to 44.43 when relevant entities along the reasoning chain are supplied, but falls to 18.56 with irrelevant entity information. For Vicuna, differentiation drops from 46.76 to 35.04 when the parent entity's information is added. Related context can therefore assist a missing connection or strengthen the wrong association.

These results concern the tested 2023 models, biological entities, and particular prompting conditions. They do not establish a permanent limit on learning novel facts. They instead show why evaluation should track understanding, separation from similar entities, and connection to existing knowledge individually. The paper also finds sensitivity to structured versus natural-language presentation, so success depends partly on how new knowledge is communicated.

Research summary

With the rapid development of NLP, large-scale language models (LLMs) excel in various benchmarks. However, the existing benchmarks may not adequately measure an LLM's ability to handle new knowledge. In this paper, we address the lack of benchmarks to evaluate LLMs' ability to handle new knowledge, an important issue in the age of information. We propose an approach called KnowGen that generates new knowledge by altering existing entity attributes and relationships, resulting in artificial entities that are absent from LLMs' training data. With KnowGen, we introduce a benchmark named ALCUNA to assess LLMs' abilities in knowledge understanding, differentiation, and association. We benchmark several LLMs and the results reveal that LLM performance in the face of new knowledge is not satisfactory, particularly in reasoning between new and internal knowledge. We also explore the impact of entity similarity and context on LLM understanding of new knowledge.
